<reason>Both sides argued at a high level, but CON built the cleaner path. CON pinned down what "regulated as gambling" actually entails (exclusion plus positive age verification), forced PRO in [A2.7] to accept the prohibition reading after PRO's opening had denied it, and then exposed the resulting verification dilemma: PRO's gate in [A4.1] rests on a "stated age" that gambling regulators treat as evasion, so either nothing changes or universal ID checks return. PRO's closing restated the burden-reversal frame without answering that dilemma. CON also tracked PRO's shifting criterion (stake-chance-prize → friction/delivery → tiers/near-miss reels) and showed each criterion is a design variable addressable by consumer defaults, answering PRO's Q1 directly (universal defaults need no age sorting). PRO scored real points — the "money's worth" via publisher exchange rates, the "CON builds scaffolding then denies the word" frame, and extracting CON's concession on the cash-out layer — but CON contained that concession as covering a minority of games and reframed the whisky analogy ("the harm is the wrapper, not the contents"). CON's two clipped turns are a modest execution cost but the lost material appears marginal.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's A1 in [B4.1]-[B4.2] and its crystallization in [B5.1]-[B5.2]: taking PRO's own formulation that gambling law means "you may not take this transaction unless you can show you aren't" a minor, and showing PRO's proposed gate is a self-declared age no gambling regulator accepts — leaving PRO caught between a decorative label and the universal identity checks it spent the debate denying.</best_rebuttal>
